title: Need for zkSpeed: Accelerating HyperPlonk for Zero-Knowledge Proofs
problem: Generating zero-knowledge proofs using the HyperPlonk zkSNARK protocol is prohibitively slow on CPUs, requiring minutes to hours, due to its four heterogeneous proof phases that demand large-bitwidth (255-381 bit) modular arithmetic over polynomials of degree up to 2^24. Existing ZKP accelerators target simpler protocols (Groth16, Orion, Spartan) that either require per-application trusted setups or produce large proofs, leaving HyperPlonk—which avoids both pitfalls—unaccelerated.
method: zkSpeed is a modular ASIC comprising eight dedicated hardware units: a unified SumCheck unit (handling ZeroCheck, PermCheck, and OpenCheck variants with shared modular multipliers across terms), an MSM unit based on Pippenger's algorithm with improved bucket aggregation reducing aggregation latency by 92%, a Multifunction Tree Unit (MTU) using hybrid DFS/BFS tree traversal for Build MLE, MLE Evaluate, and Product MLE, a FracMLE unit using constant-time Binary Extended Euclidean Algorithm (BEEA) with Montgomery batching (batch size 64) to amortize modular inversion costs, and an MLE Combine unit with resource sharing between sequential OpenCheck phases. Units communicate via a 4-channel shared bus; global SRAM stores compressed on-chip MLE tables (10-11x compression via binary packing), while streaming SumCheck computations flow through HBM (2 TB/s target). A full-chip simulator sweeps thousands of design configurations for Pareto-optimal area-performance tradeoffs.

title: Coach: Exploiting Temporal Patterns for All-Resource Oversubscription in Cloud Platforms
problem: Cloud platforms remain significantly underutilized across all resource types (CPU, memory, network, storage) because existing oversubscription approaches target only a single resource (typically CPU), causing the oversubscribed bottleneck to shift to other resources and leaving overall utilization low. Memory oversubscription is especially difficult because memory is non-fungible — physical pages cannot be quickly reassigned between VMs.
method: Coach introduces CoachVM, a general-purpose VM type that partitions each resource into a guaranteed portion (always allocated, PA-backed for memory) and an oversubscribed portion (allocated on demand from a shared pool, VA-backed for memory using zNUMA to deprioritize cold pages via guest NUMA policy). A prediction model (random forest regressor) predicts per-VM resource utilization in time windows (e.g., 3x8-hour daily windows) using VM configuration, weekday, subscription history, and customer-specific features, computing per-resource oversubscription rates per time window. The cluster scheduler uses these per-time-window predictions to colocate VMs with complementary temporal patterns, maximizing multiplexing savings. A per-server oversubscription agent monitors resource utilization and applies reactive mitigations (local resource reassignment) or proactive mitigations (VM migration) to prevent SLO violations when contention occurs.

title: Rethinking Key-Value Cache Compression Techniques for Large Language Model Serving
problem: KV cache compression algorithms are evaluated on naive transformer library (TRL) benchmarks with fixed response lengths, hiding three critical problems that prevent production deployment: suboptimal throughput under real serving frameworks (FlashAttention + PagedAttention), increased end-to-end latency due to compression-induced response length growth, and per-sample accuracy fragility on specific task types.
method: Empirical study evaluating four representative KV cache compression methods (KIVI for quantization, GEAR for quantization with error correction, StreamingLLM for structured sparsity, H2O for dynamic attention-score-based sparsity) under three missing evaluation dimensions: (1) Throughput analysis - benchmarks on LMDeploy (with PagedAttention+FlashAttention) and TRL across batch sizes, prompt lengths, and tensor parallelism degrees for LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-70B; (2) Length distribution analysis - measures response length shift D = (Lun - Lcs)/Lun across 1000 ShareGPT samples; (3) Negative sample analysis - defines negative samples as benign inputs where compression causes >10% accuracy drop on LongBench tasks; categorizes by task type (summarization, QA, code, few-shot, synthetic). Additionally provides three tools: throughput predictor (attention-layer profiling + Vidur runtime), length predictor (BERT-based classifier predicting response length given compression algorithm), and negative sample benchmark dataset.

title: SparseTransX: Efficient Training of Translation-Based Knowledge Graph Embeddings Using Sparse Matrix Operations
problem: Training translational knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models (TransE, TransR, TransH, TorusE) is bottlenecked by fine-grained scatter/gather operations during gradient computation (up to 40% of CPU training time), causing irregular memory access patterns, high backpropagation overhead, and large intermediate memory allocations.
method: SparseTransX reformulates translational KGE training by constructing a sparse incidence matrix A from training triplets: each row represents one triplet, with +1 in the head entity column and -1 in the tail entity column (for ht expression) or additionally +1 in the relation column offset by entity count (for hrt expression). Multiplying A (sparse, M x (N+R)) by the embedding matrix E (dense, (N+R) x d) directly computes batched (head - tail) or (head + relation - tail) expressions via a single SpMM call. Both forward and backward pass benefit: backward reduces to SpMM on the transpose A^T. Four models implemented: TransE (hrt computation, L2 norm), TransR (ht computation + per-relation projection matrix Mr applied separately), TransH (two ht computations with hyperplane projections), TorusE (hrt with torus distance). Framework uses iSpLib (CSR format, SIMD vectorized, auto-tuned) for CPU and DGL g-SpMM (COO format) for GPU. PyTorch DDP/FSDP wrappers support distributed training.

title: Context Parallelism for Scalable Million-Token Inference
problem: Long-context LLM inference (prefill of sequences up to 1M tokens) exceeds single-GPU memory and compute capacity, requiring efficient distributed strategies across many GPUs.
method: Context Parallelism (CP) partitions the input sequence across GPUs along the sequence dimension. Two ring-attention variants are developed: pass-KV (circulates Key/Value tensors across a GPU ring, each GPU holds fixed Q blocks) and pass-Q (circulates Query tensors, each GPU holds fixed KV). Load-balanced sharding uses 2N chunks per sequence to balance causal attention across N GPUs. Adaptive selection switches between pass-KV and pass-Q based on KV-cache miss rate to cover full prefill, persistent KV prefill, and decode phases.
